Although the device was designed for use in hospitals, where it has already helped surgeons to see the smallest blood vessels during operations, its makers believe that it will soon be cheap enough for ordinary clinics in the countryside, many of which have no equipment of this kind at all.
The team, which had spent four years testing the material on mice before anyone would agree to pay for a trial on humans, reported last month that the treatment, when given within six hours of the injury, reduced the damage by more than half.
What surprised the researchers was not the size of the effect but the fact that it appeared in older patients as well as younger ones, which suggests that the repair process, long thought to be lost with age, may in fact only be dormant.
The company has not yet said how much the device will cost, and the first machines, which were made by hand, are expected to remain in the two teaching hospitals where they are being tested.

Not only did the new working-from-home rule fail to reduce the number of hours that staff spent in meetings, but it also made those meetings longer, because anyone who joined online, however briefly, expected to be given the chance to speak.
It is the way the scheme was introduced, rather than the scheme itself, that explains why so many employees, who had asked for the change in the first place, now say they would rather go back to the office.
What managers often forget is that a rule which is welcomed on Monday may be resented on Friday, and that the more freedom a system appears to offer, the harder it becomes to ask for the help that it does not provide.
None of this means that flexible working is a bad idea; it means that a rule which looks generous on paper can still fail when nobody has thought about how it will feel in practice.

Dear participant,

Thank you for registering for the Northfield Teaching Conference on Saturday 14 November. I am writing to confirm two changes.

First, the venue has moved. The conference will now be held in Harrow Hall on the west campus, not in the Business School as we said in September. Harrow Hall is a ten-minute walk from the main gate, and a map is attached.

Second, please bring your own laptop. The workshop on classroom technology runs from 11:30 am to 1:00 pm and involves building a short online quiz. Computers will not be provided, and the wi-fi password will be given to you at the registration desk.

Registration opens at 9:00 am and the first talk begins at 9:30 am. Coffee and lunch are included, but please tell us before 10 November if you have any special dietary needs.

If you can no longer attend, reply to this email before Friday so that we can offer your place to someone on the waiting list. Places are limited, and the waiting list is long this year.

I look forward to seeing you on the 14th.

Kind regards,
Anna Whitfield
Conference Office

LIBRARY NOTICE
Weekend opening hours in November

Because of building work on the second floor, the library will open at 10:00 am on Saturdays and Sundays during November instead of 8:30 am. The ground-floor reading room and the self-service machines are not affected, and they will stay open until 10:00 pm as usual.

Books borrowed before 1 November may be kept for six weeks. Please use the returns box outside the main door when the library is closed.

We apologise for the noise and thank you for your patience.
Library Services
